questions.q: What four-part structure does the lesson recommend for explaining a long capstone project quickly?
options: Introduction, Body, Conclusion, Questions
Problem, Budget, Timeline, Invoice
Name, Rank, Serial Number, Date
Situation, Task, Action, Result
questions.explain: The lesson's structure is explicitly Situation, Task, Action, Result, in that order.

questions.q: How does the lesson say the 'Result' part of the answer should be framed for a training capstone?
options: As a specific average salary the role commands
It should be left out of the answer entirely
As a guaranteed real-world revenue increase
As a capability the finished program demonstrates, not as an invented dollar figure or percentage the project never actually measured
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that a fabricated business outcome is weaker and riskier than an honest capability claim, consistent with the no-invented-statistics rule.

questions.q: What does the lesson recommend doing when an interviewer asks you to 'walk me through one specific artifact'?
options: Change the subject to a different project entirely
Pick the one you know best and go deep, rather than skimming across all of them
Decline to answer because the capstone is fictional
Describe every single artifact from the capstone in equal, shallow detail
questions.explain: The lesson specifically advises picking the best-known artifact and going deep rather than skimming broadly.

questions.q: What does the lesson say to do when asked about a part of the capstone you didn't personally lead?
options: Be straightforward about whose focus it was, and name your own strongest contribution instead
Refuse to discuss the capstone any further
Say the whole capstone is confidential
Claim you led that part too, since the interviewer likely won't check
questions.explain: The lesson frames honesty about scope as protecting credibility, versus claiming credit for work that wasn't yours.

questions.q: Which earlier lesson does this lesson reference for the 'hardest decision' example about choosing an operating model?
options: Data Quality Management, Lesson 1
Data Governance Foundations, Lesson 11 (centralized, decentralized, and federated governance)
Microsoft Purview, Lesson 5
There is no such reference in the lesson
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly cites Data Governance Foundations, Lesson 11 for the centralized/decentralized/federated operating model choice.
